Below is a synthesis of techniques, systems, and trade-offs for scaling up end‑to‑end information retrieval (IR), drawing on recent research and production-style evaluations. End‑to‑end IR here refers to systems that combine a retriever (dense, sparse, or hybrid), candidate pooling, and one or more rerankers to deliver highly relevant passages or documents for applications like RAG, search engines, and QA.

# Executive summary
- Hybrid retrieval plus reranking is now a best‑practice stack for knowledge‑intensive domains, often matching top accuracy while reducing the number of passages passed to the generator and improving robustness over purely dense or purely sparse baselines.<cite id="adf130c5-0">Hybrid Search Retriever with reranking consistently outperformed dense-only and hybrid-only baselines, achieving high hit rate with fewer retrieved passages in a real-domain RAG system, aligning with literature that hybrid approaches with re-ranking yield better outcomes in complex domains</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Two‑stage pipelines with retriever plus re-ranker achieve state‑of‑the‑art performance; retrievers include sparse (BM25), dense (DPR/BPR/ColBERT/ANCE), and hybrid options, with dense methods requiring significant compute</cite><cite id="adf130c5-4">Hybrid strategies include sequential pipelines and score/rank fusion; newer query‑adaptive weighting guided by LLM relevance scoring has emerged to overcome static‑weight limitations</cite>.
- Model‑level scaling favors distilling cross‑encoder relevance into efficient retrievers (single‑vector or late‑interaction multi‑vector), as well as task‑specific pretraining and interaction modeling; inference‑time distillation can outperform standard training‑time distillation in some settings.<cite id="7d723003-1">State‑of‑the‑art knowledge distillation transfers cross‑encoder knowledge to single‑vector retrievers (TAS‑B, RocketQA, ERNIE‑Search) and to multi‑vector retrievers (SPLADEv2, ColBERTv2), with late‑interaction models focusing on token‑level interaction</cite><cite id="7d723003-3">ReFIT extends inference‑time distillation to ColBERTv2, surpassing both the ColBERTv2 retriever and reranker baseline at recall@100 on a BEIR subset</cite><cite id="7d723003-2">Decoder‑to‑encoder attention distillation aligns retrieval relevance with cross‑attention from a QA decoder, minimizing KL divergence between retrieval and target attention within a unified model</cite><cite id="7d723003-4">Task‑specific pretraining (e.g., RetroMAE) and distillation improve dense retrievers; comparisons span non‑interaction (DPR/ANCE), late‑interaction (ME‑BERT/COIL/ColBERT), and early‑interaction methods</cite>.
- System‑level scaling hinges on ANN indexing choices, chunking/sharding, and reranking integration. FAISS and HNSW‑family systems show distinct scaling regimes; careful corpus sizing avoids a “quality valley” and enables horizontal sharding beyond a few hundred thousand chunks. Operational practices like cold‑start controls, warm‑up, and cache‑then‑rerank matter for latency and stability.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-0">FAISS exhibits sublinear latency scaling (α≈0.48) while Chroma shows near‑constant‑time behavior; ingestion throughput varies with index type</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Latency and throughput (e.g., 7.7–8.4 ms, 141 QPS for Chroma; >100 QPS for PGVector at 50k scale) and variability (CV) are measured under controlled cold‑start conditions; FAISS shows strong sublinear scaling to 2.2M chunks</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">A U‑shaped quality curve appears at small corpus sizes; quality recovers as graphs mature and stabilizes near 59.7–64% similarity at 250–500k chunks per shard, with guidance to deploy ≥10k chunks and shard beyond 250–500k</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">At million–billion scale, effective designs combine IVF‑PQ or HNSW hybrids, incremental indexing, cache‑then‑rerank, hot/cold sharding, and streaming‑friendly retrieval under explicit latency/throughput budgets</cite>.
- Evaluation at scale mixes retrieval metrics with cost/latency and reranker choices; benefits of larger retrieval corpora plateau as noise increases, and LLM‑based reranking improves ranking but adds compute. Tooling like MSRS and frameworks (Rankify, EvaRAG) operationalize sparse+dense+LLM rerank stacks and report trade‑offs.<cite id="adf130c5-1">MSRS integrates BM25, multiple dense retrievers (NV‑Embed, gte‑Qwen2, GritLM‑7B, OpenAI and Google embeddings), and LLM‑based reranking over top‑20 candidates to study additional performance gains</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Rankify catalogues sparse/dense/hybrid retrievers and pointwise/pairwise reranking categories with examples (DPR, BPR, ColBERT, BGE, Contriever, ANCE)</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">EvaRAG shows mean 3.212 ns (P95 4.669 ns) latency trade‑offs across HNSW/IP/etc., with cost/token usage rising across configurations and benefits of larger retrieval datasets plateauing from medium to large sizes</cite>.

# End‑to‑end IR architectures for scale
Modern end‑to‑end IR favors a two‑stage design: an efficient retriever that prunes a corpus to a candidate set, followed by one or more rerankers that maximize relevance before generation. Empirically, hybrid sparse+dense retrievers with reranking deliver the best accuracy‑efficiency balance in complex domains, reducing irrelevant context passed to generators while preserving or improving top‑k quality.<cite id="adf130c5-0">A hybrid search retriever with reranking achieved 89% hit rate with fewer retrieved passages, outperforming dense-only and hybrid-only variants in a real application</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Two‑stage sparse/dense/hybrid retrievers plus rerankers are state‑of‑the‑art across NLP benchmarks</cite><cite id="adf130c5-4">Sequential sparse→dense and fusion‑style hybrids are common; query‑adaptive alpha tuning based on LLM relevance scoring has been introduced to improve adaptivity</cite>.

Practical stacks often combine:
- Sparse: BM25 with tuned parameters for lexical precision.<cite id="adf130c5-2">A hybrid pipeline used BM25 with k1=1.5, b=0.75, fetching top‑40 sparse candidates</cite>
- Dense: high‑quality encoder models (e.g., gte‑large‑en‑v1.5) for semantic recall.<cite id="adf130c5-0">The optimal hybrid configuration used Alibaba’s gte‑large‑en‑v1.5 embeddings, chunked text, and tuned Top‑N/Top‑K to balance accuracy and compute</cite>
- Reranking: pairwise/listwise cross‑encoder rerankers or pointwise LLM rerankers over dense/sparse candidates.<cite id="adf130c5-1">LLM‑based reranking over top‑20 dense/sparse results produced additional gains, using pointwise relevance scoring with Gemini 2.0 Flash</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Pointwise and pairwise reranking improve top results; listwise methods consider relative order across pairs</cite><cite id="adf130c5-2">An MMR‑based final reranking selected top‑8 passages from merged dense+sparse pools with chunk caps to limit context length</cite>.

# Scaling model training and serving (retrievers)
Model scaling for end‑to‑end IR proceeds along three axes: data‑driven pretraining, distillation to efficient architectures, and interaction modeling (early/late/attention‑based).

- Distillation to single‑vector and late‑interaction models: Cross‑encoder knowledge can be distilled to bottlenecks (TAS‑B, RocketQA, ERNIE‑Search) or to late‑interaction multi‑vector models (SPLADEv2, ColBERTv2), often yielding strong retrieval quality with far lower compute at serving time.<cite id="7d723003-1">Distillation from cross‑encoders to single‑vector retrievers (TAS‑B, RocketQAv2, ERNIE‑Search) and to multi‑vector retrievers (SPLADEv2, ColBERTv2) achieves state‑of‑the‑art dense retrieval; late‑interaction distillation focuses on multi‑token scoring</cite>. Inference‑time distillation can surpass training‑time distillation in some regimes: ReFIT for ColBERTv2 consistently outperforms both the base retriever and reranker baselines on BEIR‑style recall@100, reinforcing the value of dynamic, task‑driven supervision during inference.<cite id="7d723003-3">ReFIT extended to ColBERTv2 surpasses the base retriever and a 125‑shot reranker baseline on a BEIR subset using inference‑time distillation that updates query token embeddings</cite>.
- Attention‑based distillation and unified objectives: Aligning retrieval decisions with decoder cross‑attention in QA models provides a task‑grounded target distribution for training retrieval relevance, improving end‑to‑end utility without separate re‑ranking modules.<cite id="7d723003-2">Decoder‑to‑encoder attention distillation minimizes KL divergence between retrieval relevance and decoder cross‑attention, using document usefulness as supervision within a single model</cite>.
- Interaction modeling beyond late interaction: Early‑interaction and implicit interaction methods (e.g., DCE, I3) improve relevance by modeling query‑passage interaction during encoding (pseudo‑query reconstruction or explicit pseudo‑query generation), complementing classic non‑interaction (DPR/ANCE) and late‑interaction families.<cite id="7d723003-4">Early‑interaction models (DCE) and implicit interaction (I3) reconstruct pseudo‑queries or interact during encoding; comparisons span non‑interaction (DPR/ANCE), late‑interaction (ME‑BERT/COIL/ColBERT), and early‑interaction methods</cite>.

At serving time, scaling means choosing architectures that fit latency/throughput budgets while maintaining quality. Late‑interaction multi‑vector models can be more accurate but heavier; hybrid distillation (e.g., dynamic alpha) can adapt weights per query to balance accuracy and cost.<cite id="adf130c5-4">Sequential sparse→dense pipelines and adaptive hybrid fusion using LLM‑based relevance scoring improve retrieval adaptability beyond static weights</cite>.

# System‑level scaling: indexing, chunking, sharding, and reranking
Operational scale requires careful indexing, chunking, and pipeline orchestration. Benchmarks across vector databases reveal distinct scaling regimes and cold‑start behaviors, with clear guidance for production sizing and sharding.

- Indexing and serving behavior: FAISS’s flat indexes scale sublinearly in query time, while HNSW‑family systems (Chroma, PGVector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, OpenSearch) show near‑constant‑time behavior and efficient warm‑up as graphs mature, translating into stable latencies and high throughput at scale.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-0">FAISS shows sublinear latency scaling (α≈0.48), Chroma near‑constant time (α≈0.02), with ingestion characteristics varying by index type</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Under cold‑start controls, Chroma achieves 7.7–8.4 ms latency and up to 141 QPS at medium scale with excellent stability (CV≈2.3%); FAISS maintains sublinear scaling to 2.2M chunks</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">HNSW warm‑up reduces latency by up to 74% from 1k→50k chunks; quality follows a U‑shaped curve, then stabilizes near 59.7–64% at 250–500k chunk sizes</cite>.
- Corpus sizing and sharding: Extremely small corpora suffer a quality “valley” due to sparse graphs; growing to ≥10k chunks improves quality and stability, but gains plateau and costs rise beyond a few hundred thousand chunks per shard, motivating horizontal sharding and hybrid index designs (IVF‑PQ/HNSW) for billion‑scale KBs.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">Deploy a minimum of 10k chunks; quality gains saturate at 250–500k per shard, suggesting horizontal sharding beyond that point</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">At million–billion scale, effective systems use IVF‑PQ/HNSW hybrids, incremental indexing, cache‑then‑rerank, hot/cold separation, and streaming‑friendly retrieval under explicit latency/throughput budgets</cite>.
- Chunking and final reranking: Chunk sizes balance semantic coherence and compute; merging dense and sparse candidate pools and applying diversity‑aware reranking reduces irrelevant overlap before generation.<cite id="adf130c5-0">Chunks of 300–700 tokens balanced coherence and compute; hybrid retrieval with reranking reduced noisy context while preserving high hit rate</cite><cite id="adf130c5-2">A practical pipeline sampled top‑20 dense + top‑40 sparse candidates, then selected final top‑8 with MMR reranking, capping total context at 1800 tokens</cite>.
- LLM‑based reranking at scale: Integrating LLMs as rerankers can further improve ranking quality but increases latency and token costs; evaluation frameworks and toolkits provide reproducible setups and ablations across retriever and reranker choices.<cite id="adf130c5-1">MSRS integrates BM25 and multiple dense models, reranking top‑20 candidates with an LLM to gain additional performance</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Reranking frameworks support pointwise and pairwise strategies with multiple dense baselines (DPR, BPR, ColBERT, BGE, Contriever, ANCE)</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">EvaRAG reports latency and cost trade‑offs across HNSW/IVF/SCANN, similarity functions, reranking strategies (fusion/hierarchical/HyDe), and rerankers (BGE, minilm), showing accuracy–cost trade‑offs and plateauing gains with larger corpora</cite>.

# Data, evaluation, and scaling laws for end‑to‑end IR
Scaling end‑to‑end models requires robust offline evaluation and principled online measurement. Evidence from large corpus benchmarks and RAG evaluation frameworks shows characteristic scaling behaviors and trade‑offs.

- Dataset size effects and saturation: As retrieval datasets grow from small to medium sizes, coverage and correctness improve (more relevant docs in pool), but gains plateau from medium to large sizes due to noise and boundary effects; semantic saturation and graph maturity also contribute to stable quality ranges.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">From 1k→50k chunks, quality recovers 27.5% toward baseline; beyond 250k chunks, similarity stabilizes near 59.7% (FAISS)/64% (HNSW), indicating saturation and model resolution ceilings</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">As retrieval datasets grow, coverage/correctness/faithfulness improve up to a plateau from medium to large sizes, with SCANN/L2 showing weaker scalability</cite>.
- Hybrid evaluation stacks: Multi‑source evaluations combine sparse and dense retrievers, multiple dense encoder families, and LLM reranking to quantify incremental gains and robustness across domains and prompts.<cite id="adf130c5-1">MSRS explicitly compares BM25, NV‑Embed, gte‑Qwen2, GritLM‑7B, OpenAI and Google embeddings, and LLM‑based reranking to measure additional gains</cite>.
- Latency and cost trade‑offs: Production‑style measurements show clear P95 differences across index/similarity/rerank configurations; inference pipelines must balance accuracy with cost and token usage. Tooling reports mean P95 latencies and token budgets per configuration to support cost‑aware scaling choices.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Chroma achieves ~7.7–8.4 ms and up to 141 QPS with low variability; ingestion consistency improves dramatically with outlier removal</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">Latency varies with index and rerank choices; mean latency ~3.21 ns (P95 ~4.67 ns) with clear accuracy–cost trade‑offs; token usage rises with more complex rerankers and larger candidate pools</cite>.

# Deployment patterns and operational considerations
- Cold start and warm‑up: Controlled ingestion and retrieval under cold‑start conditions are critical to separate transient indexing effects from steady‑state performance; outlier‑robust statistics and warm‑up periods stabilize latency and throughput before scaling up.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Cold‑start protocols with N=10 sampling, outlier removal, and warm‑up reveal stable regimes (e.g., 7.7–8.4 ms latency, 123× improvement in ingestion CV)</cite>.
- Hybrid index design and incremental updates: IVF‑PQ or HNSW hybrids, incremental indexing, and streaming‑aware updates support billion‑scale corpora with bounded memory and latency budgets; hot/cold sharding separates frequently accessed vs. archival content to reduce tail latency.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">At million–billion scale, systems adopt IVF‑PQ/HNSW hybrids, incremental indexing, cache‑then‑rerank, hot/cold sharding, and streaming‑friendly retrieval under explicit latency/throughput budgets</cite>.
- Cache‑then‑rerank and diversity: To reduce per‑query cost, some pipelines cache dense vectors and rerank only when needed (cache‑then‑rerank), apply diversity (e.g., MMR) to avoid redundancy, and use chunk caps to bound context sent to the generator.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">Cache‑then‑rerank pipelines are a recommended pattern for latency/throughput efficiency at scale</cite><cite id="adf130c5-2">MMR reranking with diversity and max context caps limits redundancy and cost while preserving top‑k quality</cite>.
- Query routing and adaptive fusion: Query‑adaptive hybridization (dynamic alpha) based on relevance scoring improves recall at fixed cost, and adaptive strategies can switch between sparse, dense, or both depending on domain, language, or query type.<cite id="adf130c5-4">Dynamic alpha tuning (DAT) adjusts hybrid weights per query using LLM‑based relevance scoring, addressing static‑weight limitations in hybrid retrieval</cite>.

# Practical scaling playbook
- Choose a hybrid retriever stack with proven efficiency: BM25 for lexical precision plus a modern dense retriever (e.g., DPR/BPR/ANCE/ColBERT/Contriever variants) for semantic recall; combine with a fast pairwise/listwise reranker or an LLM pointwise reranker applied to a small candidate pool.<cite id="adf130c5-0">Hybrid retrieval with reranking reduced noisy context and achieved top hit rate using gte‑large‑en‑v1.5 embeddings and tuned Top‑N/Top‑K</cite><cite id="adf130c5-1">Integrating BM25 with multiple dense models and LLM‑based reranking yields additional gains; setup details include top‑20 candidate pools for reranking</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Two‑stage retriever–reranker pipelines are widely adopted and effective across benchmarks</cite>.
- Distill and pretrain for efficiency: Distill cross‑encoders into single‑vector or late‑interaction models; consider attention‑based objectives that align retrieval with downstream task supervision; adopt inference‑time distillation when training‑time distillation is insufficient.<cite id="7d723003-1">Cross‑encoder distillation to single‑vector and late‑interaction models (TAS‑B, RocketQA, ERNIE‑Search, SPLADEv2, ColBERTv2) achieves strong quality</cite><cite id="7d723003-2">Attention‑based distillation aligns retrieval relevance with decoder cross‑attention within a unified model</cite><cite id="7d723003-3">Inference‑time distillation (ReFIT) can surpass training‑time distillation for ColBERTv2 on BEIR subsets</cite>.
- Index and shard for stability and cost: Start with ≥10k chunks; adopt IVF‑PQ or HNSW hybrids; measure sublinear/constant‑time regimes (FAISS, Chroma, PGVector) under your workload; warm up graphs; shard beyond 250–500k chunks per shard; implement hot/cold strategies and incremental updates for streaming data.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">Deploy ≥10k chunks to avoid a quality valley; quality stabilizes near 59.7–64% at 250–500k per shard, motivating horizontal sharding</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-0">FAISS sublinear scaling vs. Chroma near‑constant‑time behavior informs hardware and index choice</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Chroma/PGVector/FAISS show stable latencies and high QPS under cold‑start controls, with large reductions in warm‑up latency</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">Hybrid indexing, incremental updates, cache‑then‑rerank, and hot/cold sharding are recommended for million–billion scale</cite>.
- Optimize final ranking and context: Use diversity‑aware MMR or listwise methods; cap total context; and apply query‑adaptive fusion (e.g., LLM‑guided alpha) to improve recall at fixed cost before generation.<cite id="adf130c5-2">MMR reranking selected top‑8 from merged dense+sparse pools with a 1800‑token cap</cite><cite id="adf130c5-4">Dynamic alpha tuning with LLM‑based relevance scoring improves adaptivity in hybrid retrieval</cite>.
- Measure end‑to‑end with latency and cost: Adopt evaluation frameworks that report P95 latency, throughput, token/call cost, and recall across retrieval, reranking, and correctness/faithfulness; expect diminishing returns as corpus size increases and plan for hybrid rerankers’ compute footprint.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">EvaRAG reports P95 latencies, token usage, and trade‑offs across indices, rerankers, and reranking strategies, showing saturation and cost–accuracy trade‑offs</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Throughput and variability under controlled conditions provide practical guidance for capacity planning</cite>.

# Caveats and open challenges
- Quality–latency–cost triability: Faster indexing (e.g., IVF) or flat designs (FAISS) improve throughput but can trade precision; HNSW offers high recall with warm‑up but may have higher P95; LLM reranking boosts ranking quality but adds cost and latency that must be bounded by budgets.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-0">FAISS sublinear scaling and Chroma near‑constant‑time behavior reflect different latency footprints across index families</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">LLM reranking yields accuracy gains but increases P95 and token usage; optimal configurations vary by metric (retrieval precision vs. efficiency)</cite>.
- Cold start and data freshness: Vector ingestion and graph warm‑up affect early‑stage quality; streaming updates must maintain index coherence without degrading recall or latency SLAs.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Cold‑start controls and outlier removal reveal transient behaviors; warm‑up reduces latency substantially</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">Streaming‑friendly retrieval with hot/cold sharding is recommended to maintain SLAs at scale</cite>.
- Evaluation saturation and domain shift: Retrieval quality saturates as corpora grow, with diminishing marginal value; hybridization and adaptive reranking can mitigate but not eliminate noise from larger pools; cross‑vendor embeddings and rerankers require careful ablation to reflect real cost/serving constraints.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">Similarity stabilizes near 59–64% beyond 250k chunks per shard, indicating saturation</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">Benefits plateau from medium to large datasets; trade‑offs vary by reranker and similarity function</cite><cite id="adf130c5-1">Comparisons across multiple dense retrievers and LLM reranking highlight cross‑vendor variability and incremental gains</cite>.

In summary, scaling end‑to‑end IR is a systems problem as much as a model‑training problem: hybrid sparse+dense retrievers with dynamic reranking, distillation to efficient architectures, and carefully engineered ANN indexing and sharding, all evaluated under production‑style latency and cost constraints, enable accurate, robust, and cost‑effective large‑scale retrieval for real‑world applications.<cite id="adf130c5-0">Hybrid retrieval with reranking improved hit rate with fewer retrieved passages in a deployed RAG setting</cite><cite id="7d723003-1">Distillation from cross‑encoders to efficient single‑vector and late‑interaction retrievers is a mainstay for scaling quality</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-2">Latency/throughput benchmarks across vector databases provide actionable guidance for production sizing and index selection</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">Evaluations that jointly track latency, cost, and retrieval quality expose the core trade‑offs and saturation effects that inform scaling decisions</cite>.

Title: Rankify: A Comprehensive Python Toolkit for Retrieval, Re-Ranking, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Snippet: Information retrieval (IR) systems [19,99] are fundamental to many natural language processing (NLP) applications [64,110], including question-answering [5,47], search engines [24,114], and knowledgebased generation [65]. These systems often rely on a two-stage pipeline: a retriever that efficiently identifies a set of candidate documents and a re-ranker that refines these results to maximize relevance to the query [4,78,91,120]. This approach has proven highly effective, with retrieval and re-ranking methods achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse NLP benchmarks. 

Retrievers form the backbone of information retrieval systems by identifying a subset of documents relevant to a user's query. The retrieval landscape includes sparse, dense, and hybrid methods. Sparse retrievers, such as BM25 [92], rely on exact term matching by representing queries and documents as high-dimensional sparse vectors. These methods are highly effective when query terms closely align with document content but struggle to capture semantic relationships. Dense retrievers, including models like DPR [120], BPR [117], ColBERT [96], BGE [15], Contriever [40] and ANCE [115], overcome this limitation by encoding queries and documents into low-dimensional dense vectors using neural networks, enabling retrieval based on semantic similarity even when lexical overlap is minimal. However, dense retrieval requires significant computational resources for training and inference. Hybrid retrieval methods [17,118] integrate the strengths of both approaches, combining the precision of sparse retrievers with the semantic understanding of dense models to achieve a more balanced and robust retrieval system. 

Re-ranking techniques enhance the initial retrieval results by ensuring the most relevant documents appear at the top. These methods are categorized into three main approaches: (1) Pointwise reranking [6,7,78,94] treats reranking as a regression or classification task, assigning independent relevance scores to each document. 

(2) Pairwise reranking [39,85,100] refines ranking by comparing document pairs and optimizing their relative order based on relevance. However, this approach treats all document pairs equally, sometimes improving lower-ranked results at the expense of topranked ones.
</snippet>

Snippet: Vector databases are a critical component of modern RAG systems, yet their scale performance characteristics are not sufficiently characterized. All databases are evaluated using identical embeddings and Top-k retrieval parameters, with cold-start conditions enforced to eliminate cross-run caching effects. # End‑to‑end IR architectures for scale
Modern end‑to‑end IR favors a two‑stage design: an efficient retriever that prunes a corpus to a candidate set, followed by one or more rerankers that maximize relevance before generation. # Scaling model training and serving (retrievers)
Model scaling for end‑to‑end IR proceeds along three axes: data‑driven pretraining, distillation to efficient architectures, and interaction modeling (early/late/attention‑based).

# System‑level scaling: indexing, chunking, sharding, and reranking

- Corpus sizing and sharding: Extremely small corpora suffer a quality “valley” due to sparse graphs; growing to ≥10k chunks improves quality and stability, but gains plateau and costs rise beyond a few hundred thousand chunks per shard, motivating horizontal sharding and hybrid index designs (IVF‑PQ/HNSW) for billion‑scale KBs.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">Deploy a minimum of 10k chunks; quality gains saturate at 250–500k per shard, suggesting horizontal sharding beyond that point</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-3">At million–billion scale, effective systems use IVF‑PQ/HNSW hybrids, incremental indexing, cache‑then‑rerank, hot/cold separation, and streaming‑friendly retrieval under explicit latency/throughput budgets</cite>.
- Chunking and final reranking: Chunk sizes balance semantic coherence and compute; merging dense and sparse candidate pools and applying diversity‑aware reranking reduces irrelevant overlap before generation.<cite id="adf130c5-0">Chunks of 300–700 tokens balanced coherence and compute; hybrid retrieval with reranking reduced noisy context while preserving high hit rate</cite><cite id="adf130c5-2">A practical pipeline sampled top‑20 dense + top‑40 sparse candidates, then selected final top‑8 with MMR reranking, capping total context at 1800 tokens</cite>.
- LLM‑based reranking at scale: Integrating LLMs as rerankers can further improve ranking quality but increases latency and token costs; evaluation frameworks and toolkits provide reproducible setups and ablations across retriever and reranker choices.<cite id="adf130c5-1">MSRS integrates BM25 and multiple dense models, reranking top‑20 candidates with an LLM to gain additional performance</cite><cite id="adf130c5-3">Reranking frameworks support pointwise and pairwise strategies with multiple dense baselines (DPR, BPR, ColBERT, BGE, Contriever, ANCE)</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">EvaRAG reports latency and cost trade‑offs across HNSW/IVF/SCANN, similarity functions, reranking strategies (fusion/hierarchical/HyDe), and rerankers (BGE, minilm), showing accuracy–cost trade‑offs and plateauing gains with larger corpora</cite>.

# Data, evaluation, and scaling laws for end‑to‑end IR
Scaling end‑to‑end models requires robust offline evaluation and principled online measurement. Evidence from large corpus benchmarks and RAG evaluation frameworks shows characteristic scaling behaviors and trade‑offs.

- Dataset size effects and saturation: As retrieval datasets grow from small to medium sizes, coverage and correctness improve (more relevant docs in pool), but gains plateau from medium to large sizes due to noise and boundary effects; semantic saturation and graph maturity also contribute to stable quality ranges.<cite id="b9ed2bfa-1">From 1k→50k chunks, quality recovers 27.5% toward baseline; beyond 250k chunks, similarity stabilizes near 59.7% (FAISS)/64% (HNSW), indicating saturation and model resolution ceilings</cite><cite id="b9ed2bfa-4">As retrieval datasets grow, coverage/correctness/faithfulness improve up to a plateau from medium to large sizes, with SCANN/L2 showing weaker scalability</cite>.

(2024), who also observed that hybrid approaches with re-ranking mechanisms tend to yield better retrieval outcomes in complex information domains. Title: Rankify: A Comprehensive Python Toolkit for Retrieval, Re-Ranking, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Snippet: Information retrieval (IR) systems [19,99] are fundamental to many natural language processing (NLP) applications [64,110], including question-answering [5,47], search engines [24,114], and knowledgebased generation [65]. These systems often rely on a two-stage pipeline: a retriever that efficiently identifies a set of candidate documents and a re-ranker that refines these results to maximize relevance to the query [4,78,91,120]. This approach has proven highly effective, with retrieval and re-ranking methods achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse NLP benchmarks. 

Retrievers form the backbone of information retrieval systems by identifying a subset of documents relevant to a user's query. The retrieval landscape includes sparse, dense, and hybrid methods. Sparse retrievers, such as BM25 [92], rely on exact term matching by representing queries and documents as high-dimensional sparse vectors. These methods are highly effective when query terms closely align with document content but struggle to capture semantic relationships. Dense retrievers, including models like DPR [120], BPR [117], ColBERT [96], BGE [15], Contriever [40] and ANCE [115], overcome this limitation by encoding queries and documents into low-dimensional dense vectors using neural networks, enabling retrieval based on semantic similarity even when lexical overlap is minimal. However, dense retrieval requires significant computational resources for training and inference. Hybrid retrieval methods [17,118] integrate the strengths of both approaches, combining the precision of sparse retrievers with the semantic understanding of dense models to achieve a more balanced and robust retrieval system. 

Re-ranking techniques enhance the initial retrieval results by ensuring the most relevant documents appear at the top. These methods are categorized into three main approaches: (1) Pointwise reranking [6,7,78,94] treats reranking as a regression or classification task, assigning independent relevance scores to each document. 

(2) Pairwise reranking [39,85,100] refines ranking by comparing document pairs and optimizing their relative order based on relevance. However, this approach treats all document pairs equally, sometimes improving lower-ranked results at the expense of topranked ones.

Title: QuDAR: Query-Wise Dual-Perspective Adaptive Retrieval
Snippet: To combine the complementary strengths of sparse and dense retrieval, a variety of hybrid strategies have been proposed. The sequential pipeline retrieves candidates with a sparse model and reranks them with a dense retriever (Santhanam et al., 2021), while score-or rank-fusion combines their outputs using fixed weights or reciprocal rank rules (Cormack et al., 2009;Bruch et al., 2023). While effective, these strategies generally rely on static weights, limiting adaptability. More recently, Dynamic Alpha Tuning (DAT) (Hsu and Tzeng, 2025) has been introduced to adjust weights per query using LLM-based relevance scoring. However, such query-adaptive methods remain relatively underexplored, and most hybrid retrieval continues to depend on fixed weighting schemes.

Specifically, the Hybrid Search Retriever with reranking not only matched the top Hit Rate but did so by retrieving fewer context passages, thereby reducing the amount of irrelevant or noisy information presented to the generative model. 

The optimal configuration was built using Alibaba's gte-large-en-v1.5 embedding model, which is known for its robust semantic retrieval capabilities. We incorporate both sparse and dense retrievers, along with LLM-based reranking, into our retrieval framework. 

Sparse Retrievers. Sparse retrievers compute the relevance of a document to a query based on the frequency of overlapping terms. We use BM25 (Robertson et al., 1994) as a representative and widely used approach in this family. 

Dense Retrievers. Dense retrievers embed both documents and queries in a shared embedding space. This provides a more flexible and context-aware approach to measuring the relatedness of text strings. We employed multiple different dense retrievers for our experiments: NV-Embed (Lee et al., 2025), gte-Qwen2-instruct (Li et al., 2023), GritLM-7B (Muennighoff et al., 2024), Promptriever (Weller et al., 2025), OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models,2 and Google's gemini-embedding-exp-03-07. 3 We provide retrieval implementation details in Appendix §D.1.

Information retrieval (IR) systems [19,99] are fundamental to many natural language processing (NLP) applications [64,110], including question-answering [5,47], search engines [24,114], and knowledgebased generation [65]. These systems often rely on a two-stage pipeline: a retriever that efficiently identifies a set of candidate documents and a re-ranker that refines these results to maximize relevance to the query [4,78,91,120]. This approach has proven highly effective, with retrieval and re-ranking methods achieving state-of-the-art performance across diverse NLP benchmarks. 

Retrievers form the backbone of information retrieval systems by identifying a subset of documents relevant to a user's query. The retrieval landscape includes sparse, dense, and hybrid methods. Sparse retrievers, such as BM25 [92], rely on exact term matching by representing queries and documents as high-dimensional sparse vectors. These methods are highly effective when query terms closely align with document content but struggle to capture semantic relationships. Dense retrievers, including models like DPR [120], BPR [117], ColBERT [96], BGE [15], Contriever [40] and ANCE [115], overcome this limitation by encoding queries and documents into low-dimensional dense vectors using neural networks, enabling retrieval based on semantic similarity even when lexical overlap is minimal. However, dense retrieval requires significant computational resources for training and inference. Hybrid retrieval methods [17,118] integrate the strengths of both approaches, combining the precision of sparse retrievers with the semantic understanding of dense models to achieve a more balanced and robust retrieval system. 

Re-ranking techniques enhance the initial retrieval results by ensuring the most relevant documents appear at the top. These methods are categorized into three main approaches: (1) Pointwise reranking [6,7,78,94] treats reranking as a regression or classification task, assigning independent relevance scores to each document. 

(2) Pairwise reranking [39,85,100] refines ranking by comparing document pairs and optimizing their relative order based on relevance. However, this approach treats all document pairs equally, sometimes improving lower-ranked results at the expense of topranked ones.

While effective, these strategies generally rely on static weights, limiting adaptability. More recently, Dynamic Alpha Tuning (DAT) (Hsu and Tzeng, 2025) has been introduced to adjust weights per query using LLM-based relevance scoring. However, such query-adaptive methods remain relatively underexplored, and most hybrid retrieval continues to depend on fixed weighting schemes.

Overview and definitions

- End-to-end retrieval performance can be improved by three levers: (i) more model parameters (stronger discriminators and readers), (ii) more training data for the retrieval side (more positive/negative pairs or more documents to index), and (iii) a larger index corpus (more documents/chunks available to retrieve). <cite id="7aa21fc4-3">Modular RAG decouples retriever and generator, allowing the corpus to be scaled independently of the generator, and advances like ANCE/Contriever make retrieval over very large corpora feasible</cite>.

What most improves end-to-end retrieval: a comparative synthesis

- Corpus/index scaling often delivers large gains in open-domain RAG across benchmarks, and can rival or exceed the benefits of moving to a larger generator in many regimes. <cite id="7aa21fc4-0">With Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 14B parameters and ClueWeb22 retrieval, enlarging the corpus consistently improved RAG; a 1.7B model with 4× larger corpus outperformed a 4B model, and a 4B model with 2× larger corpus consistently outperformed an 8B model</cite>. <cite id="7aa21fc4-1">Across multiple open-domain QA benchmarks, corpus scaling strengthened RAG and in many cases matched gains from moving to a larger model tier, with diminishing returns at larger scales; mid-sized generators paired with larger corpora often rivaled much larger models with smaller corpora, and mid-sized models tended to gain the most</cite>. <cite id="7aa21fc4-3">Prior work has implicitly moved toward increasingly large corpora (e.g., LoTTE, BEIR), yet the direct impact of corpus growth and its interaction with model size was not systematically examined until very recently</cite>.

- Model parameter scaling remains a strong, monotonic lever for end-to-end retrieval quality, especially when corpus coverage is fixed. <cite id="a6247c69-2">Self-Retrieval shows that as LLM size increases, end-to-end retrieval performance improves monotonically on NQ, TriviaQA, MS MARCO, and retrieval-augmented generation tasks</cite>. <cite id="a6247c69-1">Scaling LLMs from 30M to 3B parameters consistently improved performance over parametric-only baselines across reasoning, scientific QA, and open-domain QA</cite>. <cite id="7aa21fc4-0">However, larger generators incur higher inference and deployment overhead, and corpus-side scaling can partially offset smaller generators</cite>.

- Training data scaling for retrieval improves effectiveness via power-law-like behavior and can yield high returns per additional unit, particularly for embedding models used as retrievers. <cite id="c49c0a4c-1">Experiments on dense retrieval scaling show that scaling model size and dataset size enhance effectiveness and optimize training; robustness also adheres to a precise power-law scaling relationship with both model size and dataset size</cite>. <cite id="c49c0a4c-4">Dense retrieval scaling-law studies explicitly examine how model size, annotated training data size, and annotation types influence performance</cite>. <cite id="c49c0a4c-0">New “joint scaling laws” for embedding dimension, model size, and data provide accurate predictions of retrieval performance and isolate the role of embedding dimension as a controllable variable</cite>. <cite id="c49c0a4c-3">Embedding dimension fundamentally constrains retriever capacity; higher dimensions improve separability but increase memory and compute, directly affecting index storage and retrieval cost</cite>.

Why studies disagree: mechanisms and contexts

Title: To Memorize or to Retrieve: Scaling Laws for RAG-Considerate Pretraining
Snippet: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves language model (LM) performance by providing relevant context at test time for knowledge-intensive situations. However, the relationship between parametric knowledge acquired during pretraining and non-parametric knowledge accessed via retrieval remains poorly understood, especially under fixed data budgets. In this work, we systematically study the trade-off between pretraining corpus size and retrieval store size across a wide range of model and data scales. We train OLMo-2-based LMs ranging from 30M to 3B parameters on up to 100B tokens of DCLM data, while varying both pretraining data scale (1-150x the number of parameters) and retrieval store size (1-20x), and evaluate performance across a diverse suite of benchmarks spanning reasoning, scientific QA, and open-domain QA. We find that retrieval consistently improves performance over parametric-only baselines across model scales and introduce a three-dimensional scaling framework that models performance as a function of model size, pretraining tokens, and retrieval corpus size. This scaling manifold enables us to estimate optimal allocations of a fixed data budget between pretraining and retrieval, revealing that the marginal utility of retrieval depends strongly on model scale, task type, and the degree of pretraining saturation. Our results provide a quantitative foundation for understanding when and how retrieval should complement pretraining, offering practical guidance for allocating data resources in the design of scalable language modeling systems.
</snippet>

Title: Self-Retrieval: End-to-End Information Retrieval with One Large Language Model
Snippet: As illustrated in Figure 1, Self-Retrieval consolidates the separate components of an IR system -indexing, retrieval, and reranking -into the parameters of a single LLM. For indexing, the corpus is internalized into the LLM's parameters through self-supervised learning, enabling the model to encode and store corpus information within its internal representations. During retrieval, Self-Retrieval leverages its encoded knowledge of the corpus to semantically match the input query and directly generates the relevant documents as outputs. To ensure the generated documents exactly match those in the original corpus, we employ the constrained decoding algorithm [10,8,24] based on the trie of the corpus. For reranking, Self-Retrieval performs selfassessment on the retrieved documents to evaluate their relevance. The output score is used to rerank the retrieved passages. Moreover, for downstream tasks such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), Self-Retrieval integrates the reader component into the model, enabling direct answer generation following retrieval. Through this end-to-end approach, Self-Retrieval fully leverages LLMs' powerful capabilities in language understanding, matching, assessment, and generation to achieve unified information retrieval. 

We evaluate Self-Retrieval on three representative retrieval benchmarks: NQ, TriviaQA, and MS MARCO. Experimental results demonstrate that Self-Retrieval substantially outperforms existing sparse retrieval, dense retrieval, and generative retrieval methods on both document-level and passagelevel retrieval tasks. Furthermore, our experiments on retrieval-augmented generation tasks reveal that Self-Retrieval considerably enhances downstream performance. Additionally, larger LLMs lead to progressively better performance in Self-Retrieval, showing clear scaling benefits. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Self-Retrieval across different retrieval tasks and application scenarios. 

The potential impacts of this paper may include the following aspects. First, we introduce Self-Retrieval, an end-to-end architecture that consolidates the entire information retrieval system within a single large language model. This unified approach demonstrates substantial performance improvements over existing IR methods. Second, the corpus internalization and indexing mechanism of Self-Retrieval establishes a new paradigm to memorize, organize and retrieve the learned documents (at least part of them) during the pre-training phase, paving the way for more transparent and trustworthy text generation from LLMs.
</snippet>

Snippet: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [6,17] augments large language models (LLMs) with retrieved evidence and is widely used for open-domain question answering (QA) [8,28,30]. In parallel, the retriever determines what evidence is available to the generator and can help mitigate hallucinations [17,25], yet how retrieverside scaling interacts with generator scale is not well understood. 

We study this interaction by varying the retrieval corpus scale while holding the retrieval pipeline and evidence budget fixed. Concretely, we combine randomly-shardable retrieval over ClueWeb22 [20] with open-source Qwen3 models [33] spanning 0.6B-14B parameters, and evaluate on NQ, TriviaQA, and WebQ [1,13,16]. Our results show that enlarging the corpus consistently improves RAG and can, in this setting, partially offset smaller generators: for example, a 1.7B model with a 4× larger corpus outperforms a 4B model, and a 4B model with a 2× larger corpus consistently outperforms an 8B model. 

Overall, our work characterizes a corpus-generator trade-off in RAG and provides empirical guidance on (i) when corpus scaling can match gains from scaling the generator, (ii) which model-size regimes benefit most from additional corpus, and (iii) why these gains arise, via analyses of answer-bearing evidence coverage and context utilization.

Title: Less LLM, More Documents: Searching for Improved RAG
Snippet: A substantial body of research has focused on enhancing the intrinsic capabilities of LLMs. Instruction tuning [31,34] and prompt engineering [9,22] improve alignment with user queries, while scaling model size generally yields higher accuracy across diverse tasks [3,14]. However, ever-larger LLMs (e.g., PaLM with 540B parameters [4]) incur prohibitive computational costs, which limits their practicality in many settings. 

In parallel, retrieval-augmented models have emerged as an alternative path to scaling. Retrieval-augmented language models (RALMs) such as RETRO [2] and Atlas [12] demonstrate that enlarging inference-time datastores consistently improves performance: relatively small generators paired with massive retrieval memory can outperform much larger LM-only baselines. Shao et al. [24] further confirmed this monotonic trend. Unlike modular RAG, which decouples retriever and generator, RALMs integrate retrieval through pretraining-time vector memories, requiring retriever-generator co-training. In contrast, we focus on modular RAG with a fixed evidence budget and study corpus-generator trade-offs across model-size regimes, rather than monotonic retrieval scaling in integrated RALMs. 

Modular RAG instead relies on external corpora that can be scaled independently of the generator. This line of work has progressed from Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) [15] to efficiency-oriented methods such as ANCE [32] and Contriever [11], which make retrieval over very large corpora feasible. These advances enabled a shift from early Wikipedia-only setups to broader and more diverse corpora such as LoTTE [23] and BEIR [27]. However, while the community has implicitly moved toward increasingly larger corpora, the direct impact of corpus growth itself has not yet been systematically and comprehensively examined. 

More recently, studies have begun to explore broader factors influencing RAG, including model size, corpus scale, and context size [18,29]. However, these analyses remain fragmented and primarily descriptive, typically isolating single variables. Importantly, they do not provide a principled understanding of how corpus size and LLM size interact, leaving the corpus-generator trade-off essentially unexplored.

Title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
Snippet: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a standard technique for improving factual accuracy in language models (Lewis et al., 2020;Guu et al., 2020). By retrieving relevant passages from an external corpus and conditioning generation on them, RAG systems can reduce hallucination and provide up-to-date information. The appeal of combining small, efficient models with powerful retrieval is particularly strong for deployment on edge devices, in cost-constrained settings, and for privacy-sensitive applications. 

However, existing RAG evaluations focus primarily on large models (>10B parameters), leaving an important question largely unexplored: can smaller language models actually make effective use of retrieved information? 

Prior work has shown that irrelevant context degrades LLM performance (Shi et al., 2023;Yoran et al., 2024), but this conflates two distinct failure modes: (1) the retriever returning unhelpful passages, and (2) the model failing to utilize helpful passages. Mallen et al. (2023) investigate when retrieval helps based on entity popularity, but do not isolate the model's ability to extract from context. To separate retrieval quality from utilization, we introduce an oracle condition in which the provided passages are guaranteed to contain the answer-an experimental setting that has not been systematically examined across model scales. 

Our goal in this research is diagnostic. Instead of proposing a new RAG method, we aim to measure the utilization bottleneck quantitatively, providing an empirically grounded target for future work on fine-tuning, architectural design, or selective retrieval. 

To study this question, we evaluate five model sizes (360M to 8B parameters) from three architecture families under four retrieval conditions (none, BM25, dense, oracle) on 1,000 questions drawn from Natural Questions and HotpotQA.

Title: On the Scaling of Robustness and Effectiveness in Dense Retrieval
Snippet: Dense retrieval models have achieved state-of-the-art effectiveness, which reflects overall performance under normal conditions. But they inherit vulnerabilities commonly associated with general neural networks [24,26,40,60], making them inherently disadvantaged in terms of robustness in abnormal situations, such as handling outof-distribution (OOD) data or adversarial attacks [27,29,38,44,51]. Due to this limitation, dense retrieval models face a trade-off between robustness and effectiveness [30,38,44,59,60]. Understanding the interplay between these two aspects is critical for ensuring reliable ranking performance across diverse practical scenarios.

Our analysis focuses on the impact of two key factors, i.e., model size and dataset size, on robustness performance. Following [6], we employ the contrastive entropy metric to assess the performance of dense retrieval models. Experiments are conducted using dense retrieval models implemented with various pre-trained language models, with nonembedding parameter sizes ranging from 0.5 to 87 million. These models are trained on Chinese and English web search datasets, with training dataset sizes varying from 30K to 480K. Our results show that robustness also adheres to a precise power-law scaling relationship w.r.t. both model size and dataset size. Title: Scaling Laws for Embedding Dimension in Information Retrieval
Snippet: Dense retrieval has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neural information retrieval (IR) due to its effectiveness and simplicity. By encoding queries and documents into a shared latent space, biencoder architectures [15,36] enable efficient retrieval over massive corpora using maximum inner product search (MIPS). However, the scope of dense retrieval has recently expanded beyond simple topical matching to include more sophisticated tasks such as instruction following and multi-step reasoning. As these tasks grow in complexity, the inherent limitations of the underlying data structure, i.e., fixed-dimensional vectors, become of increasing importance. 

Previous work has shown that the capacity of a dense retriever is fundamentally constrained by the geometry of its embedding space. Theoretical analyses have demonstrated that the ability of a model to perfectly separate relevant documents from a non-relevant set is strictly bounded by the embedding dimension  [17,31]. For a corpus of size  >  + 1, there exist relevance patterns that cannot be represented by any linear similarity function. Despite these theoretical insights, the empirical relationship between embedding dimensionality and retrieval effectiveness has not been systematically quantified in the same way that model parameters or training data have been characterized through scaling laws [6,14]. 

Though exploring the scaling behavior of embedding dimensions provides useful insight to existing theories, understanding how retrieval performance scales with embedding dimension is not just a theoretical exercise; it is a practical tool for system design as demonstrated by the impact of prior scaling laws [8,14]. As an example of the impact scaling laws can have, the Chinchilla scaling laws proposed by Hoffmann et al. [8] showed that for a limited compute budget an optimally trained model has both compute and data scaled equally. This finding allowed the Chinchilla model to outperform the existing Gopher model with 20% of the parameters and broadly empowered more efficient large language model training. Additionally, scaling laws enable experiments to be done at a small scale while being able to directly predict the outcome on a scaled up version. 

As shown by the impact of prior scaling laws, being able to understand and predict how different parameters impact performance is an essential tool for building effective and efficient models. For dense retrieval efficiency, the choice of embedding dimension  directly dictates the storage footprint of the document index and the computational cost of retrieval.
</snippet>

- Corpus/index scaling often delivers large gains in open-domain RAG across benchmarks, and can rival or exceed the benefits of moving to a larger generator in many regimes. <cite id="7aa21fc4-0">With Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 14B parameters and ClueWeb22 retrieval, enlarging the corpus consistently improved RAG; a 1.7B model with 4× larger corpus outperformed a 4B model, and a 4B model with 2× larger corpus consistently outperformed an 8B model</cite>. <cite id="7aa21fc4-1">Across multiple open-domain QA benchmarks, corpus scaling strengthened RAG and in many cases matched gains from moving to a larger model tier, with diminishing returns at larger scales; mid-sized generators paired with larger corpora often rivaled much larger models with smaller corpora, and mid-sized models tended to gain the most</cite>. <cite id="7aa21fc4-3">Prior work has implicitly moved toward increasingly large corpora (e.g., LoTTE, BEIR), yet the direct impact of corpus growth and its interaction with model size was not systematically examined until very recently</cite>.

Several methodologies have been devised to facilitate this integration, but each comes with limitations that restrict its effectiveness. 

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that enhances LLMs by leveraging external corpora to retrieve relevant chunks of information (Lewis et al., 2020). However, RAG Figure 1: Overlap match of the words between ground truth and predictions of various KV cache compression methods compared to RAG on a synthetic corpus with 32k tokens. Our Few-Shot compression approach achieves results exceeding RAG when the context length is much smaller than the corpus size. 

is most effective in scenarios with narrow, focused queries that require a few pieces of evidence. When dealing with broader queries that demand synthesizing insights from multiple sources across the corpus, retrieval mechanisms may fall short (Barnett et al., 2024). This happens because retrieval typically relies on similarity-based search, which may fail to capture implicit relationships between distant pieces of evidence, making it challenging to surface all relevant context and often introducing noise or redundancy (Yu et al., 2024). Researchers have begun to address these issues, e.g., via improved chunking and pruning strategies (Edge et al., 2024), but handling broad queries with RAG remains challenging.

This progress opens up the possibility of processing entire corpora as input, offering a compelling alternative to retrieval-based meth- ods. However, this approach comes with significant computational costs, as handling large inputs requires substantial memory resources, particularly on GPUs, which creates a scalability bottleneck (Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, as the context grows, models often struggle to identify the relevant pieces of information buried in all the clutter (Liu et al., 2024). 

To bridge the gap between massive corpora and limited context windows, researchers are developing compression techniques that condense or filter input text (Jha et al., 2024).

Title: To Memorize or to Retrieve: Scaling Laws for RAG-Considerate Pretraining
Snippet: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves language model (LM) performance by providing relevant context at test time for knowledge-intensive situations. However, the relationship between parametric knowledge acquired during pretraining and non-parametric knowledge accessed via retrieval remains poorly understood, especially under fixed data budgets. In this work, we systematically study the trade-off between pretraining corpus size and retrieval store size across a wide range of model and data scales. We train OLMo-2-based LMs ranging from 30M to 3B parameters on up to 100B tokens of DCLM data, while varying both pretraining data scale (1-150x the number of parameters) and retrieval store size (1-20x), and evaluate performance across a diverse suite of benchmarks spanning reasoning, scientific QA, and open-domain QA. We find that retrieval consistently improves performance over parametric-only baselines across model scales and introduce a three-dimensional scaling framework that models performance as a function of model size, pretraining tokens, and retrieval corpus size. This scaling manifold enables us to estimate optimal allocations of a fixed data budget between pretraining and retrieval, revealing that the marginal utility of retrieval depends strongly on model scale, task type, and the degree of pretraining saturation. Our results provide a quantitative foundation for understanding when and how retrieval should complement pretraining, offering practical guidance for allocating data resources in the design of scalable language modeling systems.

Title: Self-Retrieval: End-to-End Information Retrieval with One Large Language Model
Snippet: As illustrated in Figure 1, Self-Retrieval consolidates the separate components of an IR system -indexing, retrieval, and reranking -into the parameters of a single LLM. For indexing, the corpus is internalized into the LLM's parameters through self-supervised learning, enabling the model to encode and store corpus information within its internal representations. During retrieval, Self-Retrieval leverages its encoded knowledge of the corpus to semantically match the input query and directly generates the relevant documents as outputs. To ensure the generated documents exactly match those in the original corpus, we employ the constrained decoding algorithm [10,8,24] based on the trie of the corpus. For reranking, Self-Retrieval performs selfassessment on the retrieved documents to evaluate their relevance. The output score is used to rerank the retrieved passages. Moreover, for downstream tasks such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), Self-Retrieval integrates the reader component into the model, enabling direct answer generation following retrieval. Through this end-to-end approach, Self-Retrieval fully leverages LLMs' powerful capabilities in language understanding, matching, assessment, and generation to achieve unified information retrieval. 

We evaluate Self-Retrieval on three representative retrieval benchmarks: NQ, TriviaQA, and MS MARCO. Experimental results demonstrate that Self-Retrieval substantially outperforms existing sparse retrieval, dense retrieval, and generative retrieval methods on both document-level and passagelevel retrieval tasks. Furthermore, our experiments on retrieval-augmented generation tasks reveal that Self-Retrieval considerably enhances downstream performance. Additionally, larger LLMs lead to progressively better performance in Self-Retrieval, showing clear scaling benefits. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Self-Retrieval across different retrieval tasks and application scenarios. 

The potential impacts of this paper may include the following aspects. First, we introduce Self-Retrieval, an end-to-end architecture that consolidates the entire information retrieval system within a single large language model. This unified approach demonstrates substantial performance improvements over existing IR methods. Second, the corpus internalization and indexing mechanism of Self-Retrieval establishes a new paradigm to memorize, organize and retrieve the learned documents (at least part of them) during the pre-training phase, paving the way for more transparent and trustworthy text generation from LLMs.

Incorporating external information into large language models (LLMs) significantly enhances their utility across various applications, enabling them to generate more informed and accurate outputs. Several methodologies have been devised to facilitate this integration, but each comes with limitations that restrict its effectiveness. 

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that enhances LLMs by leveraging external corpora to retrieve relevant chunks of information (Lewis et al., 2020). However, RAG Figure 1: Overlap match of the words between ground truth and predictions of various KV cache compression methods compared to RAG on a synthetic corpus with 32k tokens. Our Few-Shot compression approach achieves results exceeding RAG when the context length is much smaller than the corpus size. 

is most effective in scenarios with narrow, focused queries that require a few pieces of evidence. When dealing with broader queries that demand synthesizing insights from multiple sources across the corpus, retrieval mechanisms may fall short (Barnett et al., 2024). This happens because retrieval typically relies on similarity-based search, which may fail to capture implicit relationships between distant pieces of evidence, making it challenging to surface all relevant context and often introducing noise or redundancy (Yu et al., 2024). Researchers have begun to address these issues, e.g., via improved chunking and pruning strategies (Edge et al., 2024), but handling broad queries with RAG remains challenging. 

Recent advancements have extended LLMs' ability to process longer contexts, pushing the boundaries of how much information they can handle simultaneously (Team et al., 2024;Li et al., 2025a). This progress opens up the possibility of processing entire corpora as input, offering a compelling alternative to retrieval-based meth- ods. However, this approach comes with significant computational costs, as handling large inputs requires substantial memory resources, particularly on GPUs, which creates a scalability bottleneck (Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, as the context grows, models often struggle to identify the relevant pieces of information buried in all the clutter (Liu et al., 2024). 

To bridge the gap between massive corpora and limited context windows, researchers are developing compression techniques that condense or filter input text (Jha et al., 2024).

Our results provide a quantitative foundation for understanding when and how retrieval should complement pretraining, offering practical guidance for allocating data resources in the design of scalable language modeling systems.

Title: Less LLM, More Documents: Searching for Improved RAG
Snippet: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [6,17] augments large language models (LLMs) with retrieved evidence and is widely used for open-domain question answering (QA) [8,28,30]. While much prior work improves RAG by scaling the generator, larger models typically incur higher inference and deployment overhead [7,19,21]. In parallel, the retriever determines what evidence is available to the generator and can help mitigate hallucinations [17,25], yet how retrieverside scaling interacts with generator scale is not well understood. 

We study this interaction by varying the retrieval corpus scale while holding the retrieval pipeline and evidence budget fixed. Concretely, we combine randomly-shardable retrieval over ClueWeb22 [20] with open-source Qwen3 models [33] spanning 0.6B-14B parameters, and evaluate on NQ, TriviaQA, and WebQ [1,13,16]. Our results show that enlarging the corpus consistently improves RAG and can, in this setting, partially offset smaller generators: for example, a 1.7B model with a 4× larger corpus outperforms a 4B model, and a 4B model with a 2× larger corpus consistently outperforms an 8B model. 

Overall, our work characterizes a corpus-generator trade-off in RAG and provides empirical guidance on (i) when corpus scaling can match gains from scaling the generator, (ii) which model-size regimes benefit most from additional corpus, and (iii) why these gains arise, via analyses of answer-bearing evidence coverage and context utilization.

Snippet: A substantial body of research has focused on enhancing the intrinsic capabilities of LLMs. Instruction tuning [31,34] and prompt engineering [9,22] improve alignment with user queries, while scaling model size generally yields higher accuracy across diverse tasks [3,14]. In contrast, we focus on modular RAG with a fixed evidence budget and study corpus-generator trade-offs across model-size regimes, rather than monotonic retrieval scaling in integrated RALMs.

More recently, studies have begun to explore broader factors influencing RAG, including model size, corpus scale, and context size [18,29]. Title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
Snippet: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a standard technique for improving factual accuracy in language models (Lewis et al., 2020;Guu et al., 2020). By retrieving relevant passages from an external corpus and conditioning generation on them, RAG systems can reduce hallucination and provide up-to-date information. The appeal of combining small, efficient models with powerful retrieval is particularly strong for deployment on edge devices, in cost-constrained settings, and for privacy-sensitive applications. 

However, existing RAG evaluations focus primarily on large models (>10B parameters), leaving an important question largely unexplored: can smaller language models actually make effective use of retrieved information? 

Prior work has shown that irrelevant context degrades LLM performance (Shi et al., 2023;Yoran et al., 2024), but this conflates two distinct failure modes: (1) the retriever returning unhelpful passages, and (2) the model failing to utilize helpful passages. Mallen et al. (2023) investigate when retrieval helps based on entity popularity, but do not isolate the model's ability to extract from context. To separate retrieval quality from utilization, we introduce an oracle condition in which the provided passages are guaranteed to contain the answer-an experimental setting that has not been systematically examined across model scales. 

Our goal in this research is diagnostic. Instead of proposing a new RAG method, we aim to measure the utilization bottleneck quantitatively, providing an empirically grounded target for future work on fine-tuning, architectural design, or selective retrieval. 

To study this question, we evaluate five model sizes (360M to 8B parameters) from three architecture families under four retrieval conditions (none, BM25, dense, oracle) on 1,000 questions drawn from Natural Questions and HotpotQA.

documents.title: Can Small Language Models Use What They Retrieve? An Empirical Study of Retrieval Utilization Across Model Scale
documents.snippet:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a standard technique for improving factual accuracy in language models (Lewis et al., 2020;Guu et al., 2020). By retrieving relevant passages from an external corpus and conditioning generation on them, RAG systems can reduce hallucination and provide up-to-date information. The appeal of combining small, efficient models with powerful retrieval is particularly strong for deployment on edge devices, in cost-constrained settings, and for privacy-sensitive applications. 

However, existing RAG evaluations focus primarily on large models (>10B parameters), leaving an important question largely unexplored: can smaller language models actually make effective use of retrieved information? 

Prior work has shown that irrelevant context degrades LLM performance (Shi et al., 2023;Yoran et al., 2024), but this conflates two distinct failure modes: (1) the retriever returning unhelpful passages, and (2) the model failing to utilize helpful passages. Mallen et al. (2023) investigate when retrieval helps based on entity popularity, but do not isolate the model's ability to extract from context. To separate retrieval quality from utilization, we introduce an oracle condition in which the provided passages are guaranteed to contain the answer-an experimental setting that has not been systematically examined across model scales. 

Our goal in this research is diagnostic. Instead of proposing a new RAG method, we aim to measure the utilization bottleneck quantitatively, providing an empirically grounded target for future work on fine-tuning, architectural design, or selective retrieval. 

To study this question, we evaluate five model sizes (360M to 8B parameters) from three architecture families under four retrieval conditions (none, BM25, dense, oracle) on 1,000 questions drawn from Natural Questions and HotpotQA.

Title: On the Scaling of Robustness and Effectiveness in Dense Retrieval
Snippet: Dense retrieval models have achieved state-of-the-art effectiveness, which reflects overall performance under normal conditions. But they inherit vulnerabilities commonly associated with general neural networks [24,26,40,60], making them inherently disadvantaged in terms of robustness in abnormal situations, such as handling outof-distribution (OOD) data or adversarial attacks [27,29,38,44,51]. Due to this limitation, dense retrieval models face a trade-off between robustness and effectiveness [30,38,44,59,60]. Theoretical analyses have demonstrated that the ability of a model to perfectly separate relevant documents from a non-relevant set is strictly bounded by the embedding dimension  [17,31]. Though exploring the scaling behavior of embedding dimensions provides useful insight to existing theories, understanding how retrieval performance scales with embedding dimension is not just a theoretical exercise; it is a practical tool for system design as demonstrated by the impact of prior scaling laws [8,14]. As an example of the impact scaling laws can have, the Chinchilla scaling laws proposed by Hoffmann et al. [8] showed that for a limited compute budget an optimally trained model has both compute and data scaled equally. This finding allowed the Chinchilla model to outperform the existing Gopher model with 20% of the parameters and broadly empowered more efficient large language model training.
